chunks.text: ## Deliberate decisions visible in the code Decision Current implementation Benefit and trade-off --- --- --- Separate learning and community systems Main API uses MongoDB; LMS API uses PostgreSQL. Their models and tokens are distinct. Keeps learning transactions and community data independently owned; adds cross-service identity and operational complexity. Server-side identity hand-off Main API returns a hashed, expiring, single-use SSO code; the LMS verifies it server-to-server and issues its own JWT. Avoids sharing passwords or treating one service's token as the other's; requires coordinated configuration and integration tests. Domain-appropriate persistence MongoDB documents model community records and embedded chat messages; relational LMS tables model course, enrollment, and progress relationships. Fits the current access patterns; each approach has scaling constraints (document growth versus relational migrations and query design). Provider calls stay behind services Sarvam and optional Google Translate are called by the main API; Razorpay and YouTube credentials are used by the LMS API. Keeps provider secrets out of browser code and lets APIs enforce provider-specific validation and limits. Chat delivery is not held up by translation The original chat message is persisted and delivered before the optional translation result. Translation latency/failure does not block the core message; an in-process follow-up is less durable than a persistent job queue. Payment is verified by the server The LMS creates Razorpay orders and verifies the returned signature using a server-side secret. The browser does not decide payment success; payment state and enrollment still need consistent, retry-safe transitions. LMS schema changes have migration history Alembic migrations are present for PostgreSQL. Provides reviewable, ordered schema changes; startup create all() should not become a substitute for migrations. API role checks are server-side FastAPI dependencies enforce LMS roles; the main API has admin middleware. API boundaries, rather than UI visibility, decide access; main admin identification is currently a hard-coded email and needs centralization.

chunks.heading: Practices to preserve
chunks.text: ## Practices to preserve - Keep data ownership explicit. Do not directly read or write another service's database. Add a versioned API contract or a deliberate event integration when cross-domain data is needed. - Keep secrets server-side. Browser environment variables are public by design. Payment, SSO, database, Sarvam, and Drive credentials must remain in the owning service's secret manager. - Validate authorization at the API. Frontend route guards improve UX but do not replace authenticated, role-checked API operations. - Use short-lived, single-use credentials for hand-offs. The current SSO design avoids passing a long-lived main token to the LMS. - Treat database migrations as reviewed code. Create and inspect an Alembic migration for PostgreSQL schema changes; consider indexes, TTL behavior, backfills, and rollback plans for MongoDB changes. - Preserve graceful provider degradation. Translation and audio are auxiliary to sending the original message. Keep provider timeouts bounded and return a clear product state when an optional provider is unavailable. - Keep demo behavior unmistakable. Sample scores and fallback leaderboard rows must never be presented as real learner assessment or live competition results. - Document cross-service contracts. SSO URLs, role mappings, token ownership, browser origins, payment states, and route versions need one named owner and automated compatibility checks.

chunks.heading: Gaps and practices to correct
chunks.text: Gap observed Why it matters Recommended correction --- --- --- Main and LMS browser tokens are stored in localStorage . Any successful script injection in the origin can read bearer tokens. Assess an HTTP-only, Secure, SameSite cookie/BFF design. If tokens remain browser-accessible, reduce lifetime where practical, enforce strict output escaping and CSP, and avoid storing additional sensitive data there. Plan migration and CSRF protections rather than changing cookie behavior piecemeal. Main admin access is tied to a hard-coded email; LMS roles are separate. Access changes are coupled to code and role mapping can drift between services. Use explicit, auditable admin grants with least privilege; centralize the policy per service, define provisioning/revocation, log privileged actions, and test SSO role mapping. LMS startup attempts create all() and suppresses exceptions. A schema/startup failure can be hidden, and runtime schema creation competes with migration ownership. Make migrations the deployment gate. Fail readiness clearly on required database errors; remove silent exception suppression after deployment behavior is verified. LMS practice evaluation returns fixed sample results; challenge fallback data can look real. Users and downstream systems may mistake demonstration data for model output or live rankings. Keep these routes disabled or explicitly labeled as demo until backed by real evaluation and persisted challenge state. Add tests that reject sample fallbacks in production mode. Main Voice Challenge submissions are Drive files without durable submission records or consent/script metadata. Filename-based duplicate detection is fragile; audit, deletion, review, and retry workflows are difficult. Add a submission record with owner, language/challenge, consent version and timestamp, script, Drive file ID, processing/review state, and retention/deletion policy. Enforce an appropriate unique key in the database. Translation retry/deduplication state is partly process-local, and TTS audio is embedded in chat documents. Process restarts can lose retry state; embedded base64 audio can increase document size and backup/transfer cost. Move asynchronous translation to a durable queue/outbox with idempotent jobs. Measure document growth; if material, store audio in object storage and persist a reference with expiry. The main frontend and backend have documented route and behavior mismatches; REST and Socket.IO origin lists differ. A UI can silently lose a feature, and a deployment can work for HTTP but fail for sockets. Add contract/integration tests for critical routes and a shared origin policy or deployment validation that checks both transports. Backend automated test coverage is limited or absent in the inspected manifests. Authorization, payment, SSO, migration, and provider regressions may escape frontend/build checks. Establish service-level unit and integration test suites before making high-risk changes; run them in CI with disposable/test databases and stubbed providers. Some state has two possible owners (for example LMS API streak records and frontend-local streak state). Users can see inconsistent or device-specific results. Name one system of record per feature. Move reads/writes through that owner and add a migration plan for client-held data if it must be retained.

chunks.text: Recommended evolution: 1. Normalize language identifiers and index the fields used for candidate filtering. Verify index use with representative query plans; avoid loading every profile into application memory. 2. Fetch a bounded candidate set using database predicates, then apply deterministic ranking only to eligible candidates. 3. Do not introduce collaborative filtering or a learned ranking model until there is consented interaction data, an offline evaluation set, bias checks, and a rollback path.

chunks.heading: Catalogs, jobs, and leaderboards
chunks.text: ### Catalogs, jobs, and leaderboards - Use database-side filtering, stable ordering, and bounded pagination for course/job lists. Prefer keyset pagination for large or frequently changing result sets; use composite indexes that match measured filters and sort order. Keep a maximum page size. - Use explicit deterministic ordering for leaderboards, including a tie-break rule. Compute rankings from persisted real results; a static fallback must be identified as sample data, not merged into production results. - Add indexes from observed query plans and workload metrics, not by indexing every field. Every index adds write and storage cost. - Use a persistent queue or transactional outbox when a task must survive restarts (translation retries, email, media review). Make consumers idempotent, bound retries, and expose terminal failures for operations.

chunks.heading: Service structure
chunks.text: ### Service structure - Keep the existing Next.js, Express, and FastAPI stacks unless a concrete limitation justifies a migration. Framework churn is not a substitute for clearer boundaries or tests. - Within each API, prefer a modular-monolith structure: route/controller for transport concerns, service for domain rules, repository/query layer where persistence logic is reused, and schema/model for validation and storage. Avoid both giant controllers and unnecessary layers for trivial operations. - Treat OpenAPI and typed request/response schemas as contracts. Generate or share TypeScript types where feasible; add compatibility tests for high-value flows rather than duplicating unverified interfaces. - Keep synchronous APIs for request/response work. Add asynchronous infrastructure only for work requiring durable retries, fan-out, or latency isolation; document ownership, idempotency, dead-letter handling, and operational alerts before launch.

chunks.heading: Delivery lifecycle
chunks.text: ### Delivery lifecycle 1. Plan: state the user outcome, service/data owner, API changes, privacy impact, failure modes, and measurable acceptance criteria. Record significant cross-service decisions as short Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), including alternatives and revisit conditions. 2. Implement: make a small vertical change with input validation, authorization, observable errors, migration(s), and backward-compatible contracts. Do not bundle unrelated cleanup. 3. Test: use fast unit tests for domain rules; integration tests for database, auth, and provider boundaries; contract tests for frontend/API and SSO; and a small end-to-end set for signup, course purchase/enrollment, and chat. Stub external providers in ordinary CI. 4. Review: require peer review and extra security/payment review for authentication, authorization, PII, payments, file uploads, migrations, and retention changes. Review generated migrations and API compatibility. 5. Release: deploy schema changes in an expand/contract sequence when old and new application versions may overlap. Use staging and a canary or phased rollout for risky changes; keep a rollback or forward-fix plan. 6. Operate: monitor latency, error rate, queue age, payment reconciliation, provider failures, and database health. impact, failure modes, and measurable acceptance criteria. Record
significant cross-service decisions as short Architecture Decision Records

authorization, observable errors, migration(s), and backward-compatible
contracts. Do not bundle unrelated cleanup.
3. **Test:** use fast unit tests for domain rules; integration tests for
database, auth, and provider boundaries; contract tests for frontend/API
and SSO; and a small end-to-end set for signup, course purchase/enrollment,
and chat. Stub external providers in ordinary CI.
4. **Review:** require peer review and extra security/payment review for
authentication, authorization, PII, payments, file uploads, migrations,
and retention changes. Review generated migrations and API compatibility.
5. **Release:** deploy schema changes in an expand/contract sequence when
old and new application versions may overlap. Use staging and a canary or
phased rollout for risky changes; keep a rollback or forward-fix plan.
6. **Operate:** monitor latency, error rate, queue age, payment reconciliation,
provider failures, and database health. Use request/correlation IDs without
logging tokens, credentials, or unnecessary personal data. Feed incidents
and support reports into follow-up work.

chunks.text: ### Main entity notes - User: email/password or Google identity; primary/secondary learning languages; known languages with fluency; learner/teacher role; location; translation preference; optional profile and learning counters. - Match: ordered user pair, status, and seven-day expiry. A unique index applies to ordered (user1,user2) ; the controller also checks both pair directions. The TTL index deletes pending/rejected records, not accepted ones. - Chat: participants and an embedded message array. blockedBy controls blocking; deletedBy hides a chat per participant; clearedAt stores each user's message-history cutoff. A new message can restore a hidden chat while retaining the caller's prior cutoff. - Message: original text, sender, timestamp, read flag, optional translated text/language, and cached base64 TTS audio. Audio is embedded in MongoDB; moving it to object storage would require an API/data migration. - Notification: match/message notification types with recipient/sender and optional match/chat references. Current unread-count behavior counts all recipient notifications. - Report: reporter, reported user, associated chat, reason, timestamp. Reports are intentionally preserved by connection reset; bulk deletion is a separate admin operation. - Job: language/proficiency/type, compensation, company/location, responsibilities, requirements, contact email, poster, view count, status, expiry. A TTL index removes it 30 days after expiry. - Language: published/draft guide, slug, native name, script, regions, roadmap and embedded typed resources. - SSOCode: only a hash is stored; the raw code is returned to the browser, expires in 60 seconds, and is consumed once.
